chunks: He said: Abu al-Hasan Ali ibn Malik al-Nahwi narrated to us from Muhammad ibn al-Fadhl, from Abu Abdillah Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Katib, from Yamut ibn al-Muzarra', from Isa ibn Ismail, from al-Asma'i, from Isa ibn Umar, saying:

Dhu al-Rummah, the poet, held the view of negation regarding divine intervention in human acts, while Ru'bah ibn al-Ajjaj held the view of affirmation. One day, they met at Bilal ibn Abi Burdah's court, the governor of Basrah. Bilal urged them to debate. Ru'bah said: 'By God, a bird does not dig its nesting place, nor does a predator find its den, except by the decree and destiny of God.' Dhu al-Rummah replied: 'By God, God did not permit the wolf to take the milch-animal of a poor, afflicted family.' Ru'bah said: 'Did the wolf take it by its own will, or by the will of God?' Dhu al-Rummah said: 'Rather, by its own will and desire.' Ru'bah said: 'This, by God, is a lie against the wolf!' Dhu al-Rummah said: 'By God, a lie against the wolf is lesser than a lie against the Lord of the wolf.'

Then he said: And Abu al-Hasan Ali ibn Malik al-Nahwi recited to me verses by Mahmud al-Warraq: 'O censurer, I did not commit sins out of ignorance, nor were they another's doing, nor mine; nor out of insolence toward God, nor because my ignorance overcame my intellect; but I hold favourable expectation of the forgiveness of the One peerless in gracious deeds and bounty. If my expectation proves true, in His bounty is confirmation for one like me; and if punishment befalls me, it came by way of fairness in judgment and justice.'

key_terms.الاثبات: Affirmation -- affirming divine decree over all acts
key_terms.النفي: Negation -- denying divine predestination of human acts

ai.seo_question: What is the debate between Dhu al-Rummah and Ru'bah ibn al-Ajjaj about free will and divine decree?
ai.summary: This narration records a celebrated theological debate between two famous Umayyad-era Arab poets: Dhu al-Rummah, who denied divine intervention in human acts, and Ru'bah ibn al-Ajjaj, who affirmed it. Their exchange took place before the governor of Basrah, using vivid animal metaphors to argue about God's role in worldly events. It concludes with poetry by Mahmud al-Warraq that takes a middle path: acknowledging personal responsibility for sins while placing hope in God's unique capacity for forgiveness and justice.
